h1: The 8 Best NAS Storage Devices of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best NAS Storage Devices 2026: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: eight diskless NAS boxes from Synology and UGREEN, from simple 2-bay backup hubs to 4-bay and 6-bay media servers.
summary: The UGREEN DXP4800 Plus is the best NAS for most buyers, with four bays and a five-core Intel chip aimed at 4K media. Synology's DS925+ wins if software polish and support matter more. The DXP6800 Plus gives six bays, while the DS223 is the cheapest entry. Remember that drives cost extra with every model.
intro: Every NAS on this page ships empty. That one fact changes the shopping math: the figure on the listing is only the enclosure, and the drives you add can cost as much as the box itself. The number of bays then decides how far the investment can stretch before you have to buy another unit.

We reviewed eight diskless NAS units from Synology and UGREEN and ranked them on bay count, processor, memory, software ecosystem and fit for a home or small office. Our source is the spec sheets and listing details alone, so we say little about speed in daily use and focus on what the hardware and software promise on paper.

products.name: UGREEN NAS DXP4800 Plus
products.verdict: Four bays and a 5-core Intel chip aimed at 4K media.
products.description:
The UGREEN DXP4800 Plus is a four-bay diskless NAS built on an Intel Pentium Gold 8505 with five cores, in the $500+ tier. The listing positions it for strong 4K transcoding.

It takes first place because the hardware list is the best balance in the group. Four bays leave room to grow, and the Intel processor suits a media server. The Synology DS925+ matches the bay count and brings a more mature software platform, but gives you less on paper to justify its price. The DXP4800 GT swaps in an AMD chip with more memory.

Buy it if you stream and back up media at home. The caveat is that drives are sold separately, so budget for them. UGREEN's software is also younger than Synology's, which matters if you value long-established polish.

products.name: Synology DS925+
products.verdict: Synology's current-generation 4-bay with the DSM ecosystem.
products.description:
The Synology DS925+ is a four-bay diskless NAS running DSM, Synology's software ecosystem, in the $500+ tier. The listing calls it the current-generation DiskStation.

It ranks second because UGREEN's top pick lists stronger hardware, yet the DS925+ answers with a software suite that many people consider the benchmark for home NAS use. A current-generation model also has a longer support runway than the older DS425+ below, which makes it a safer bet for a device meant to last years.

Buy it if software polish and long-term support matter most. The tradeoff is that you pay a premium tier price without leading the group on processing power. Drives are sold separately, as they are on every unit here. If you simply want the most hardware for the money, the DXP4800 Plus is the stronger value.
products.idealFor: Buyers who prize DSM and support.
products.skipIf: You want the most CPU for the money.

products.name: UGREEN NAS DXP6800 Plus
products.verdict: Six bays and an Intel i3 for big libraries.
products.description:
The UGREEN DXP6800 Plus is a six-bay desktop NAS with an Intel i3 1215U six-core CPU, in the $500+ tier. It has the highest bay count and capacity ceiling in this guide.

It lands third because most homes never need six bays, and the larger body and cost come with the territory. Against the four-bay models, though, it has the most room to grow, and the i3 gives it solid processing muscle for several users at once.

Buy it for a big media library or a small office where several people share files. Skip it if four bays are plenty, since the DXP4800 Plus is cheaper and does most of the same work. As with every unit on the list, drives are not included, so six bays can turn into a sizable purchase once you fill them.

products.name: UGREEN NAS DXP4800 GT
products.verdict: The most RAM among 4-bay picks, on an AMD platform.
products.description:
The UGREEN DXP4800 GT is a four-bay desktop NAS with an AMD R2514 processor and 8GB of DDR4 RAM, in the $500+ tier. The memory is the most among the four-bay picks.

It sits fourth because the Plus lists an Intel chip with a clear transcoding focus, while the GT is built around an AMD platform. Extra RAM helps when you run several services at once, such as containers, backups and file sharing, but it does not replace media handling.

Buy it if you run many services on one box and are comfortable with AMD hardware. Skip it if your priority is Intel transcoding for video streaming, since the DXP4800 Plus fits better. Drives are sold separately, so check what the total cost looks like. Ask whether your planned apps benefit from the extra memory before paying for it.

products.name: Synology DS425+
products.verdict: A 4-bay Synology positioned as a private cloud media server.
products.description:
The Synology DS425+ is a four-bay diskless NAS with the DSM ecosystem, positioned as a private cloud media server, in the $500+ tier.

It ranks fifth because the DS925+ is the newer hardware with the same DSM platform, so the 425+ makes sense mainly if it is cheaper or easier to find. Against the UGREEN four-bay units it offers a more polished software experience, but it lists less hardware detail than the DXP4800 GT or Plus.

Buy it if you want a private cloud and trust Synology for the software. Skip it if you want the newest generation or the strongest listed processor. Drives are sold separately, and the older model may have a shorter support window than the DS925+, so factor that in. For most buyers the newer Synology is the safer pick of the two.

products.name: UGREEN NAS DXP4800 Pro
products.verdict: UGREEN's higher-tier 4-bay, with few details listed.
products.description:
The UGREEN DXP4800 Pro is a four-bay diskless NAS positioned as UGREEN's higher-tier four-bay configuration, in the $500+ tier.

It ranks sixth because the listing gives far fewer specs than the Plus, so we cannot confirm what the upgrade actually buys. A higher tier usually means better internals, but without a processor or memory figure you are guessing. Against the DXP4800 Plus, the clearer spec sheet makes the Plus the safer buy.

Buy it if you plan to grow into the platform and can verify the specs with the seller before ordering. Skip it if you need confirmed numbers, because the page does not provide them. Like the other UGREEN units, it ships without drives. Compare its full listing with the Plus and GT before you pay extra for a name that suggests more than the data shows.

products.name: Synology DS225+
products.verdict: Two bays with an Intel CPU and hardware transcoding.
products.description:
The Synology DS225+ is a two-bay diskless NAS with an Intel CPU, hardware transcoding and DSM, in the $200 to $500 tier.

It ranks seventh because two bays limit growth, and the bigger four-bay units give you more room for the money. But it costs less than any of them, and it brings the transcoding hardware that makes video streaming smoother. It sits above the DS223 because of that processor.

Buy it if you want DSM and media transcoding in a small footprint without paying for four bays. Skip it if you want to expand later, since two drives cap your capacity and redundancy options. As with every model here, drives are separate, so the total cost grows quickly. For a household that expects to keep adding files, the DS925+ is a better long-term investment.

products.name: Synology DS223
products.verdict: The simplest, cheapest real NAS here.
products.description:
The Synology DS223 is a two-bay diskless NAS positioned as a simple home and office backup hub, with DSM, in the $200 to $500 tier.

It lands last because it has the least headroom of the group, and it does not advertise media transcoding. What it has is price: it is the cheapest true entry-level NAS on the page, and the DSM software still gives you a capable backup tool. Against the DS225+, it is simpler and less capable.

Buy it if your goal is straightforward backups for a family or a small office. Skip it if you want to stream video or expect your storage needs to grow. Drives are sold separately, so remember to budget for them. If you can stretch to the DS225+, you gain a more flexible processor for little extra money.

whatMatters.detail: Bays are the slots for hard drives. More bays allow more capacity and redundancy options. The DXP6800 Plus has six, the four-bay models include the DS925+ and the DXP4800 Plus, and the DS223 has two. Check the bay number in the title, and think about how much data you will hold in three years.

The processor affects media transcoding and how smoothly the NAS handles several tasks at once. Core counts help you compare, such as the five-core Intel in the DXP4800 Plus. Look for the processor model name on the listing, and check whether hardware transcoding is mentioned if you plan to stream video.

Memory, measured in gigabytes of RAM, helps a NAS run many apps and services together. The DXP4800 GT lists 8GB of DDR4, the most among the four-bay picks. Check the listed amount, and ask whether it can be upgraded, especially if you plan to run containers or virtual machines.

Software shapes your daily experience of a NAS. The Synology units run DSM, a long-established platform with a broad app library, while UGREEN uses its own system. Check which ecosystem the listing names, and read about update policy and support length before you commit to a brand.

Diskless means the unit ships without hard drives. Every model here is diskless, so you must buy drives separately, and the cost can rival the enclosure. Look for the word diskless in the title, and add the price of drives to your budget before you compare totals.

faq.q: Do these NAS units include hard drives?
faq.a: No. Every unit here is diskless, so drives are sold separately. Plan for at least two drives on the DS223 and four on the DXP4800 Plus, and budget for them alongside the enclosure.

faq.q: What is the common NAS buying mistake?
faq.a: Counting only the box. The drives often cost as much as the NAS itself, so a model like the DXP6800 Plus becomes expensive once all six bays are filled.

faq.q: Is a 4-bay NAS worth it over 2-bay?
faq.a: If you expect to expand, yes. A four-bay such as the DS925+ leaves room to grow. For simple backups, the two-bay DS223 is enough and costs less.

faq.q: How do I set up a NAS?
faq.a: Insert the drives, connect the unit to your router and follow the setup app. Synology models like the DS925+ guide you through DSM, while UGREEN units use their own installer.

faq.q: Do I need to maintain it?
faq.a: Yes, but lightly. Update the software, check drive health periodically and keep a backup of important files elsewhere. A NAS like the DS425+ is not a substitute for off-site backups.

faq.q: Can I stream media from it?
faq.a: Several are positioned for it. The DXP4800 Plus has an Intel chip aimed at 4K transcoding, the DS425+ is pitched as a private cloud media server, and the DS225+ lists hardware transcoding.

finalTake: The UGREEN DXP4800 Plus is the best NAS for most buyers, offering four bays and a capable Intel processor. Choose the Synology DS925+ if software polish and long support matter more, and the DXP6800 Plus when you need six bays. The DS223 is the budget entry. Whatever you pick, budget for the drives.
